title: The Price-Range Question: 5 Versions + 3 Questions to Ask First
description: Ask the price-range question in writing before the sales call. 5 versions for different offers, plus the 3 questions to ask first in the reply thread.
lead: This is the price-range question from the reel, written 5 ways for different offers, plus the 3 other questions to ask in the reply thread before you book. Use them and every call on your calendar is with someone who can actually pay.
insider: Our clients want buyers on their calendar, not just meetings, so we qualify interested replies before a call is booked. In the construction software campaign below, that meant **31 sales-qualified demos and 6 signed annual contracts**. The questions are the easy part. Answering every reply fast, in the right order, is the work we do for clients.

blocks.text: The line from the reel

blocks.label: The price-range question
blocks.text: Work like this usually runs [your range]. Is that in the range you'd look at?

You know the call. Sixty minutes of discovery, a good demo, then: "Oh, that's too expensive for us." An hour gone, with someone who was never going to buy. Everyone says don't talk price early. But asking once, **in writing, before the call**, is different. It takes the prospect ten seconds to answer, and it saves you the hour.
The 3 rules

items: **Give a range, not one price.** A range like "$2,000 to $4,000 a month" feels like information, not a quote. One exact number invites haggling before you even know what they need.
**Ask in the reply thread, once they say interested.** Not in the first cold email (too early) and not on the call (too late). The moment they reply "sounds interesting", that's when.
**Yes? Book it. No? You saved an hour.** If the range works, send your booking link right away. If it doesn't, thank them, offer something smaller if you have it, and move on.

blocks.label: This won't work unless
blocks.text: Your range is honest. If you quote $2,000 to $4,000 and then pitch $9,000 on the call, you've wasted their hour and lost their trust. Use the range most of your real deals actually land in.
The 5 versions
Same idea, worded for different kinds of offers. Swap in your real numbers.
1. Monthly retainer (agencies, marketing, outsourced services)

blocks.label: Version 1: retainer
blocks.text: Happy to set up a call. Quick heads-up so I don't waste your time: most of our clients invest between [$X] and [$Y] a month, depending on [scope, e.g. how many channels]. Is that in the range you'd look at?
2. Software / SaaS (per seat or per plan)

blocks.label: Version 2: software
blocks.text: Glad it's interesting. For a team your size, plans usually come out between [$X] and [$Y] a year, depending on [users / features]. Is that roughly in budget before we book a demo?
3. One-off project (websites, builds, installs, construction)

blocks.label: Version 3: project
blocks.text: Sounds like a good fit. Projects like the one you described usually land between [$X] and [$Y], mostly depending on [size / materials / timeline]. Does that fit what you had in mind?
4. Consulting, coaching or training

blocks.label: Version 4: consulting
blocks.text: Happy to talk. So you know upfront: engagements like this usually run [$X] to [$Y] for [time period, e.g. a 3-month program]. Is that within the range you'd consider?
5. High-ticket or custom (enterprise, done-for-you, big contracts)

blocks.label: Version 5: high-ticket
blocks.text: Thanks for getting back to me. Every setup is custom, but to give you a sense: most clients at your stage start somewhere between [$X] and [$Y]. If that's in the right range, I'll send a few times for a call. If not, no problem at all, just let me know.
The 3 questions to ask first

The reel says ask price **last**, after who decides and when. Price on its own can feel blunt. After two or three easy questions, it feels like a normal part of making sure the call is worth their time. Ask these in the reply thread, one or two per message.

head: Ask in this order
Why you ask it
Good answer looks like
rows: 1. "How are you handling [the problem] right now?"
Shows if the problem is real and what you're up against
A real current process, or a pain they describe
2. "Is anyone else involved in a decision like this?"
So the right people are on the call, not just one of them
A name or a role, or "just me"
3. "Is this something you're looking to sort out this quarter, or later on?"
Tells you if it's now or someday
A time frame in the next few months
4. The price-range question (one of the 5 versions above)
Saves an hour with someone who can't pay
"Yes, that's in range" or a number close to it

blocks.text: A full reply thread, start to finish

blocks.label: Example thread (copy and adapt)
blocks.text:
PROSPECT: Sounds interesting, tell me more.

YOU: Happy to. Quick question first so I point you at the right thing: how are you handling [problem] right now?

PROSPECT: We do it in-house, but it's taking way too much of my time.

YOU: Makes sense, that's the most common reason people reach out. Is anyone else involved in a decision like this, and are you looking to sort it out this quarter or later on?

PROSPECT: Me and my business partner. Ideally before January.

YOU: Perfect. Last thing so I don't waste your time: work like this usually runs [$X to $Y a month]. Is that in the range you'd look at?

PROSPECT: Yes, that's fine.

YOU: Great. Here's my calendar, pick any 20-minute slot that works for you and your partner: [booking link]
How to read the answer

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: Putting the price in the very first cold email, before they care.
Asking price first, before any easy question.
Giving one exact number instead of a range.
A range so wide it means nothing ("$500 to $50,000").
Taking the call anyway when they said "way out of budget", hoping to change their mind.

blocks.text: Write your version with Claude

blocks.label: Price question prompt
blocks.text:
I sell: [one sentence about your offer]
Most of my real deals land between: [$X] and [$Y] [per month / per project / per year]
What makes the price go up or down: [scope, team size, timeline...]

A prospect just replied to my cold email: "[paste their reply]"

Write my next reply. It should:
1. Be under 60 words.
2. Ask how they handle [the problem] now, OR who else decides and when, if they've already answered that.
3. If they've answered both, ask the price-range question using my real range, and offer my booking link if it fits: [link].
Friendly, plain English, no pressure.

faq.q: Won't asking about price scare people off?
faq.a: Some, yes. Those are people who would have said "too expensive" at the end of an hour-long call. Losing them in the thread saves you that hour.

faq.q: What if my price really depends on the project?
faq.a: Give the range most of your deals land in and say what moves it, like "depending on size". That's still honest and useful.

faq.q: Should I ask on LinkedIn too?
faq.a: Yes, the same order works in LinkedIn messages: current situation, who decides and when, then the range.
